h1: SEO for salons and spas that turns searches into chair time
metaTitle: SEO for Salons and Spas: Bookings, Not Browsing
metaDescription: SEO for salons and spas in India. We rank treatment pages with visible price bands, then move the searcher into a booking link within a single tap.
answer: Salon and spa searchers compare price before they compare location. So the pages that win are treatment pages — keratin, balayage, bridal packages — each with a visible rupee band, the stylist who did the work, and a booking link one tap away. Everything else is a Google Business Profile problem.
takeaways: **Publish a price band or lose the tab.** Not one number — a range with the variable named, like length or product. Hiding it doesn't stop the comparison, it just moves it next door.
One page per treatment beats one page called Services. A menu row cannot rank for `keratin treatment price in Indiranagar`.
Bridal enquiries arrive two to four months before the wedding season. Publishing bridal content in November is publishing it late.
Your Google Business Profile category decides which `near me` searches you even appear in. Most salons pick it once, wrongly, and never look again.
The conversion is a booking, not a form fill. Measure click-to-WhatsApp and the booking button, or you're measuring nothing.

sections.h2: Price is the first filter. Location is the second.
body: Watch how somebody actually books a hair appointment. They search `keratin treatment near me`, open three tabs, and close the two that don't say what it costs. Distance gets checked after that, because most people will travel twenty minutes for a price they trust and nobody books blind.

Salon owners hate this. The standard objection is fair: hair length, product line and stylist seniority all move the number, so one published price is misleading. Agreed. That's an argument for publishing a band, not for publishing nothing. A line in the shape of "₹4,000–₹9,000 depending on whether your hair sits above or past the shoulder" — your numbers, not ours — answers the question, sets the expectation before the client is in the chair, and quietly filters out the person who was never going to pay it.
A page with no price doesn't prevent the comparison. It removes you from it.

callout.title: The deal-platform habit
callout.body: If every offer you run lives on a discount aggregator, you're training your own customers to search the aggregator instead of your name. The listing is rent. Your treatment pages are the asset. Run the offers, by all means — but put the same offer on a page you own, and give it a URL you can send people to.

sections.h2: One page per treatment, not one page called Services
body: The single most common structure we see is a Services page with a two-column menu and forty rows. It ranks for nothing, because a row of four words gives Google nothing to match a real query against.
Split it. Every treatment you'd happily do fifty of a month deserves its own page — and the page needs to answer what the searcher was actually worried about.

table.caption: What a treatment page has to carry, and why a menu row cannot.

What the page must answer
Why a menu row loses
rows: Price band by hair length, how long the appointment takes, how long the result lasts, aftercare rules, which product line you use.
The query contains the word 'price'. The menu row doesn't contain a price.
The actual difference in plain language, upkeep cost over a year, how each behaves on dark Indian hair, who it suits.
Comparison intent needs a comparison. A list is not one.
What each package includes, trial policy, travel and outstation charges, advance and cancellation terms, which dates are already blocked.
Bridal clients compare inclusions line by line. Adjectives don't survive that.
Price band, duration, which of your branches offer it, and a booking link that pre-selects the treatment.
Proximity queries are decided in the local pack and on the landing page — you need both.

sections.h2: The salon calendar is the content calendar
body: Demand in this business is seasonal and the seasons are known years in advance, which makes planning easier here than in almost any industry we work with. What breaks is the timing: most salons publish the festive offer during the festival and the bridal page in December.

Search runs ahead of the event. A bride books her makeup artist months before the date; someone planning a Diwali colour appointment starts looking at options weeks out. Content published on the day of demand has no time to rank.
numbered: **Bridal, eight to twelve weeks ahead of each wedding stretch.** Indian weddings cluster around auspicious dates in roughly November–February and again around April–May, and the enquiry comes long before the date.
**Festive pages, four to six weeks ahead.** Karva Chauth, Durga Puja, Diwali, Onam, Ganesh Chaturthi — whichever ones your city actually observes. Don't publish all of them everywhere.
**Keep last year's page, update the dates.** Deleting the 2025 bridal page and starting fresh throws away every link and every ranking signal it earned. Re-date it, refresh the pricing, keep the URL.

**Add the boring operational detail.** Extended hours during festive week, whether you take walk-ins, which branches stay open. That's the information people search for at 8pm the night before, and almost nobody publishes it.

sections.h2: Your stylists are the differentiator, and Google usually can't see them
body: Clients don't follow salons. They follow the person who did their colour. That loyalty is the most valuable thing you own and it is almost always invisible to search, buried in an Instagram grid that Google indexes poorly and a gallery page with forty untitled JPEGs.

Give the senior stylists real pages: what they specialise in, how long they've been cutting, training they've done, and eight to twelve photos of their own work. That's a genuine experience-and-expertise signal, which is the part of [E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t) that beauty content is judged hardest on.
Then fix the photos, because in this industry the images are the content.
bullets: **Real work, not stock.** A stock photo of a European model in a white salon tells a Bengaluru client nothing about what you can do with her hair.
**Descriptive filenames and alt text.** `global-hair-colour-burgundy-shoulder-length.jpg` beats `IMG_20260714_2.jpg`. Alt text should describe the treatment and the hair type, not stuff keywords.
**Compress everything.** Photographers hand over 6 MB files. Serve WebP or AVIF at sensible dimensions, or the page loses its Core Web Vitals fight before a single word is read.
**Before-and-after pairs, with written consent on file.** They convert harder than anything else on the site.
**Don't rely on an embedded Instagram feed.** It renders after the fact and it is not the same as having those images on your own pages.

sections.h2: The listings decide whether you appear at all
body: For `salon near me`, the map pack sits above everything and most bookings never reach a website. So the profile is the product, and one setting inside it does more damage than any other: the primary category. 'Beauty salon', 'Hair salon', 'Nail salon', 'Day spa' and 'Massage spa' pull different queries. Pick the one that matches what you actually earn most from, then add the rest as secondary.
After that it's maintenance work, and it's dull, which is why competitors don't do it.

Then there's the address problem. Salons move — a lane over, a floor up, a new landlord. The old address stays live on Justdial, on Sulekha, on a booking app you signed up to in 2022, and on Apple Maps. Inconsistent local citations are the single most common reason a well-run salon can't crack the map pack in its own neighbourhood.
bullets: One profile per branch, and one page on your site per branch. A single Contact Us page listing five addresses will not rank any of them.
Load your actual service list into the profile with prices — the booking-related fields inside the profile are underused and they show up in the panel.
Reply to every review, including the ugly ones. A calm reply to a one-star review sells better than five generic five-star ones.
Post your festive hours as a Google post before the festival, not after.
Fix the name-address-phone string everywhere it appears, then check it again every six months. It drifts.

callout.title: Where this sits in our work
callout.body: Profile setup, category strategy, citation cleanup and review workflows are part of [Google Business Profile optimisation](/services/google-business-profile-optimisation). For a single-location salon it's often the entire first month, and it's usually the month that moves the number.

sections.h2: From the search result into the chair, in one tap
body: This is where salon websites throw away the traffic they just earned. Somebody lands on your balayage page, decides yes, and gets handed a contact form with six fields and no confirmation of anything.

In India the booking almost always wants to happen on WhatsApp. So build the path deliberately: a click-to-WhatsApp button on every treatment page with the message pre-filled — "Hi, I'd like to book a balayage at your Koramangala branch" — so the person on your front desk knows the treatment, the branch and the source before they type a word.

Tag those links. A UTM parameter on each button tells you which treatment page produced which conversation, and that's the only way to prove organic search is filling chairs rather than filling a dashboard. If you run online booking software, put the booking button above the fold on the treatment page, not only in the header.

sections.h2: What it costs, how long it takes, and what we actually guarantee
body: Our SEO starts at ₹75,000 a month, and smaller sites — a single salon with a handful of treatment pages — start at ₹40,000, ex-GST. Multi-branch chains sit higher because each location needs its own profile, its own page and its own citation cleanup. Full numbers are on [pricing](/pricing), and [what local SEO costs](/cost/local-seo-cost) breaks down the map-pack side specifically.

The honest timeline: map-pack movement on a clean profile can show inside four to eight weeks, because the competition in most Indian neighbourhoods is genuinely poor at this. Treatment pages ranking for city-level price queries take three to six months. Anyone quoting faster is quoting a different problem.

We freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one — bookings and real booking conversations, not raw form fills. If we haven't beaten that number in 90 days, we keep working free until we do. We never promise a specific ranking position for a specific keyword, because nobody controls Google's index. We take three clients a month, which is the only reason that promise is survivable.

faqs.q: Do I really have to publish my salon prices online?
faqs.a: Publish a band, not a single figure. Something like "₹4,000–₹9,000 depending on hair length" answers the query, ranks for price searches your competitors ignore, and screens out enquiries you'd have lost anyway. Hiding the number doesn't stop the price comparison — it removes you from it.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to bring bookings for a salon?
faqs.a: Local-pack visibility can move in four to eight weeks if your Google Business Profile has been neglected, which it usually has. Treatment pages ranking for city-wide price queries take three to six months. Bridal and festive pages need eight to twelve weeks of lead time before the season they target.

faqs.q: Is a Google Business Profile enough, or do I need a website too?
faqs.a: For a single salon doing walk-ins, the profile does most of the work and should be fixed first. You need a site the moment you want to rank for treatment and price queries, run bridal packages, or open a second branch — the profile can't hold that detail, and it isn't an asset you own.

faqs.q: Should I list my salon on booking apps and directories?
faqs.a: Yes, for reach and for the citation value, provided the name, address and phone number match your profile exactly. What you shouldn't do is let them become your only bookable presence. A listing is rented volume; the pages and reviews attached to your own name are what still work next year.

faqs.q: How do I get more Google reviews without breaking the rules?
faqs.a: Ask every satisfied client at checkout, with a short link or QR at the desk, and reply to every review that lands. Don't offer discounts for reviews, don't filter who you ask, and never buy them — review gating and paid reviews both violate Google's policies and the profile is what gets suspended.

faqs.q: I have five branches. One website or five?
faqs.a: One website, five location pages, five Google Business Profiles. Each location page needs its own address, hours, stylists, photos and treatment availability — not a copy of the same text with the area name swapped, which is the pattern Google demotes as scaled content.
